abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel theoretical framework for analyzing global optimization problems with non-convex objective functions defined over non-convex feasible regions. Traditional optimality conditions rely heavily on convexity assumptions, which limit their applicability in practical optimization scenarios. We introduce a unified optimality theory based on the concept of local Lipschitzian minima and develop necessary and sufficient conditions that characterize global optima without requiring convexity structure. The proposed framework employs advanced tools from variational analysis and nonsmooth optimization to establish connections between local search directions and global optimality. We prove that any stationary point satisfying the new generalized Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions can be classified according to its potential for global optimality. This paradigm shift enables a fresh perspective on algorithm design, where strategies can be explicitly evaluated based on their theoretical potential to escape local minima. The framework is particularly relevant for continuous optimization problems arising in machine learning, engineering design, and operations research. Our theoretical contributions include convergence guarantees under weakened assumptions and explicit characterization of the relationship between problem structure and optimization difficulty. This work establishes a foundation for a new generation of optimization algorithms that are theoretically grounded in non-convex analysis.

We provide significant improvements to the convergence analysis of stochastic optimization algorithms, specifically addressing their asymptotic behavior on non-convex problems with relaxed regularity conditions. While existing convergence results for stochastic gradient descent methods typically assume Lipschitz continuity of gradients and bounded variance, many practical optimization problems fail to satisfy these requirements. This paper establishes tighter convergence bounds for stochastic optimization under mere continuity assumptions and unbounded gradient noise. We develop a novel martingale-based framework that yields stronger concentration inequalities for iterates generated by adaptive stochastic algorithms. The analysis reveals that previous convergence rates were overly pessimistic due to conservative technical assumptions. We prove that under the proposed generalized conditions, stochastic optimization achieves order O(1/√T) convergence to stationary points with high probability, matching lower complexity bounds up to constant factors. Furthermore, we introduce refined notions of criticality that account for the geometric properties of objective landscapes. These theoretical advances not only close gaps in the existing literature but also provide guidance for designing more efficient stochastic optimization methods. Our results have immediate implications for machine learning applications where standard assumptions are violated.

We introduce a novel hybrid optimization architecture that unifies deterministic and stochastic search strategies within a self-adaptive framework for solving large-scale global optimization problems. Existing metaheuristic approaches typically operate in isolation, either exploring the search space through population-based methods or exploiting local structures via deterministic techniques. The proposed system, called Adaptive Hierarchical Optimization Framework (AHOF), implements a multi-layered search mechanism where population-based exploration, deterministic local search, and learning-based prediction dynamically allocate computational resources based on problem characteristics detected during optimization. AHOF incorporates a machine learning component that models the fitness landscape and adaptively selects appropriate search strategies for different problem regions. The framework implements a novel memory mechanism that preserves promising solutions across algorithm restarts while maintaining diversity through niching techniques. Computational experiments on a comprehensive benchmark suite demonstrate that AHOF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in continuous, combinatorial, and multi-objective optimization contexts. The system achieves this performance through principled integration of complementary search paradigms, representing a paradigm shift in optimization algorithm design. Implementation details and open-source code are provided to facilitate reproducibility and further development.

We develop an enhanced version of the widely-used differential evolution algorithm with improved performance on multi-objective optimization problems. While differential evolution has proven effective for global optimization, its standard formulation lacks mechanisms for proper diversity maintenance and convergence to well-distributed Pareto fronts. The proposed Improved Adaptive Multi-objective Differential Evolution (IAMDE) introduces three key modifications: an adaptive parameter control scheme based on success-history experience, a novel mutation strategy that balances exploration and exploitation throughout the optimization process, and an enhanced archive management system utilizing clustering-based density estimation. IAMDE implements a hybrid local search mechanism activated when solutions approach the Pareto front, significantly accelerating convergence while preserving solution diversity. The algorithm incorporates a crowding distance modification that prioritizes solutions in under-represented regions of the objective space. Extensive experimental validation on standard multi-objective benchmark functions and real-world engineering design problems demonstrates substantial improvements over established multi-objective evolutionary algorithms. Compared to NSGA-II and MOEA/D, IAMDE achieves superior convergence and spread metrics across diverse problem characteristics. The proposed method is particularly effective for problems with complex Pareto front geometries and high-dimensional objective spaces.
